Hospital follow-up after recent admission for fever, leukocytosis, blood pressure fluctuations, and suspected infection. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Michelle King is a 39-year-old female with history of quadriplegia from prior spinal cord injury and a suprapubic catheter. She was admitted to District Regional Hospital from 06/29/2021 to 07/02/2021 with increasing spasms, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, significant constipation, and labile blood pressure accompanied by headache and vomiting. In the ED she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000. There were concerns for urinary tract infection and she was treated with IV antibiotics; however, urine cultures were “not very impressive.” She reports she hardly had a bowel movement during the hospitalization, but after discharge she had a large bowel movement and felt markedly better. She believes her episode was more likely autonomic dysreflexia triggered by severe constipation rather than a true UTI. No CT was performed during admission; x-rays were done. She notes it was very hot leading up to admission and she tends to stay indoors more during heat. 

Currently she feels back to her normal baseline and denies any pain or discomfort. She uses daily Miralax for bowel management and doubles the dose if she hasn’t gone; she has lactulose at home for rescue, which takes about two days to work and is “brutal” but effective. 

COVID-19: She is unvaccinated and hesitant due to concerns about unknown side effects and reports of “vaccine injury.” She believes she is healthy enough to recover if infected, takes vitamin C and a multivitamin, and does not get the annual flu shot. She is open-minded to discussion. 

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Recent febrile illness with leukocytosis (WBC 23,000) during hospitalization; suspected UTI vs inflammatory response from severe constipation/autonomic dysreflexia 
Assessment: Hospital course notable for fever, leukocytosis, and blood pressure lability with headache/vomiting. Treated empirically for possible UTI, but urine cultures were not convincing. Patient had significant constipation with marked improvement after a large bowel movement post-discharge, supporting constipation-triggered autonomic dysreflexia as a likely contributor. Currently asymptomatic and back to baseline. Heat/dehydration may have exacerbated constipation. 
Plan: 
- Repeat CBC in 2–3 weeks to ensure the white blood cell count trends down. 
- Encourage adequate hydration, particularly during hot weather, to reduce constipation risk. 
- Return/seek care sooner for recurrent fever, worsening spasms, diaphoresis, headache, vomiting, or blood pressure lability. 

2. Constipation, acute on chronic; likely trigger for autonomic dysreflexia 
Assessment: Longstanding bowel regimen with daily Miralax; uses lactulose as rescue. Hospitalization temporally associated with severe constipation; significant symptom relief after large bowel movement. 
Plan: 
- Continue daily Miralax as baseline regimen; may use lactulose as rescue for severe constipation as previously effective. 
- Emphasize hydration and avoiding overheating to help prevent constipation. 
- Contact clinic if no bowel movement despite regimen or if rescue therapy is needed frequently. 

3. Quadriplegia with suprapubic catheter 
Assessment: Chronic condition associated with risk for autonomic dysreflexia and UTIs. No current pain or new complaints today. 
Plan: 
- Continue current catheter care and monitoring. No antibiotics indicated at present given lack of symptoms and unimpressive urine cultures during admission. 
- Educate on warning signs: fever, new urinary symptoms, increased spasms, or symptoms of autonomic dysreflexia. 

4. Dyslipidemia screening and routine labs 
Assessment: Due for cholesterol testing; can coordinate with repeat CBC. 
Plan: 
- Schedule fasting labs in 2–3 weeks: CBC and full lipid panel. 

5. COVID-19 vaccine counseling; unvaccinated, hesitant 
Assessment: Patient is hesitant due to concerns about unknown side effects; open-minded to discussion. Given her quadriplegia, clinician considers her higher risk if infected. 
Plan: 
- Strongly recommend COVID-19 vaccination; discussed risks/benefits and that vaccination is the primary preventive measure. Patient to consider and will reach out with questions. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- Return to clinic in 2–3 weeks for fasting labs (CBC and lipid panel). Seek earlier care for recurrent fever, uncontrolled blood pressure, severe constipation not responding to regimen, or symptoms of autonomic dysreflexia or UTI.

CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Six-week postoperative follow-up after right medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Stephanie Morales (MRN 113322) is a 44-year-old female, now 6 weeks status post right medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, presenting for routine postoperative follow-up. She reports the knee is “good” with no pain and no problems other than persistent numbness on one side of the knee near the incision. She is participating in physical therapy and plans to continue. She asks about timing for return to work at UPS; her position involves going up and down steps. Her employer has asked if she can return to a seated role with breaks. She also asks about readiness to resume driving.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Status post right medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, 6 weeks 
Assessment: Doing well overall with no pain. Exam today shows healed surgical incision with mild swelling and tenderness at the incision, ROM 0–120 degrees, antalgic gait with slight limp and decreased velocity, no assistive device. Radiographs (3 views) show implants in stable position without evidence of loosening or early complications. Persistent localized cutaneous numbness likely due to expected postoperative neurapraxia; surgeon anticipates gradual improvement as cutaneous nerves heal. Early recovery phase; continued functional gains expected over the next several weeks to months. 
Plan: 
- Continue physical therapy focusing on strength, range of motion, endurance, and gait training. 
- Educated that occasional aches/pains can occur; many patients feel “back to themselves” by 2–3 months post-op. 
- No additional interventions needed today given reassuring exam and imaging.

2. Postoperative cutaneous numbness around incision (expected neurapraxia) 
Assessment: Focal sensory change adjacent to the incision, common after knee arthroplasty; expected to diminish over time as nerves recover. 
Plan: 
- Reassurance and observation; no specific treatment required at this time. 
- Continue PT; monitor for gradual reduction in numb area.

3. Gait impairment in recovery (antalgic gait with slight limp) 
Assessment: Mild antalgic pattern consistent with normal recovery at 6 weeks without assistive device. 
Plan: 
- Continue PT with emphasis on gait mechanics and progressive strengthening/endurance.

4. Return-to-work counseling (UPS) 
Assessment: Current functional status and surgeon’s restrictions are not compatible with typical UPS duties; a seated role with breaks may still conflict with restrictions. Anticipated readiness for labor-intensive work closer to 3 months post-op. 
Plan: 
- Work restrictions provided: no lifting >5–10 pounds; no standing or sitting longer than 30 minutes at a time. 
- Provided work excuse note for additional 6 weeks. 
- Reevaluate work readiness at next follow-up.

5. Driving readiness 
Assessment: Data indicate reflex times return to baseline by 6 weeks; return to driving is patient-dependent based on feeling safe and ready. 
Plan: 
- May resume driving when she feels ready and safe to do so.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Telemedicine follow-up in 6 weeks to assess progress and revisit work status. Continue PT in the meantime.

Evaluation of abnormal renal ultrasound showing an atrophic right kidney.

CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Sudden visual distortions and blurring of vision. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Emily presents reporting decreased vision when reading and that straight lines/door frames appear crooked. She also has difficulty adjusting to dim lighting (e.g., in restaurants). 1. Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration, right eye 
Assessment: Symptoms of metamorphopsia and decreased central vision. Plan:

Plan:

Post-hospital follow-up after inferior myocardial infarction with right coronary artery stent placement. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
The patient was hospitalized for 48 hours for an inferior myocardial infarction and underwent stent placement in the right coronary artery. She has been home for a couple of weeks. She reports feeling better than before hospitalization but “not perfect.” She denies any recurrent chest pain since the stent placement. The right wrist catheterization site was initially red but is healing; she believes there is no infection. She notes shortness of breath when going up and down stairs; she has otherwise been taking it easy with very light activity and no formal exercise. 

Medications: Taking ticagrelor (Brilinta) twice daily every 12 hours and baby aspirin once nightly; no cost issues. Also taking rosuvastatin (Crestor) 40 mg once daily and metoprolol succinate (Toprol) 50 mg once daily. 

Diet/Activity: She is trying to watch salt intake, eating vegetables and unsalted chicken, but has had pizza a few times on weekends and asks if that is acceptable. She asks if she can resume swimming, which she misses.

Assessment: Clinically improving without recurrent angina. Emphasized importance of dual antiplatelet therapy to prevent stent thrombosis. EF about 50% per hospital records. 
Plan: 
- Continue aspirin daily indefinitely. 
- Continue ticagrelor (Brilinta) twice daily for at least 1 year. 
- Continue rosuvastatin (Crestor) 40 mg daily. 
- Continue metoprolol succinate (Toprol) 50 mg daily.

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Right knee pain after a fall. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
The patient is a pleasant female who presents with persistent right knee pain following a fall from a tandem bicycle approximately two weeks ago. She reports landing on the right knee against a curb. Pain has been present daily since the injury; ibuprofen provides temporary relief but pain recurs. She is concerned about taking ibuprofen longer than two weeks. Pain is primarily along the medial aspect of the knee and is worse with walking uphill or on inclines. She sometimes feels the knee “shifts” or is unstable when walking and occasionally notes a click with full extension. She denies prior knee problems before this injury. She initially washed a small abrasion and applied a bandage. She has not returned to swimming since the injury; usual activities include walking her dog. 

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Right knee injury—suspected posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) sprain with mechanical symptoms 
Assessment: Mechanism (direct impact/fall onto the knee), exam today notable for medial joint line tenderness, 1+ posterior drawer on the right compared with the contralateral side, stable collateral ligaments, negative Lachman and McMurray tests, and normal patellar tracking. Plain radiographs obtained today are normal (no fracture, spurs, or joint space loss). Overall presentation is most consistent with a PCL sprain. Differential includes associated meniscal or chondral injury not excluded by exam. 
Plan: 
- Imaging: Order MRI of the right knee to evaluate the PCL and assess for meniscal or chondral injury. 
- Bracing: Fit with an off-the-shelf knee brace today for stability; custom bracing not indicated at this time. 
- Physical therapy: Refer to PT near home/work with focus on reducing swelling, restoring full range of motion, and progressive strengthening; begin with a few sessions and adjust frequency based on progress and home exercise capability.

- Prognosis/contingency: Isolated PCL injuries rarely require surgery. If MRI shows only PCL involvement, plan nonoperative management with bracing and PT. If persistent instability after a couple of months of rehab, or if MRI reveals additional injuries, will discuss surgical options. 

2. Superficial abrasion, right knee 
Assessment: Small, dime-sized abrasion over medial patella; dry and healing; no signs of infection. 
Plan: Continue local wound care as needed; no additional intervention required at this time. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- Return to clinic in 4–6 weeks to reassess symptoms, review MRI results, and evaluate stability and progress with PT. Seek earlier care if pain or instability worsens.
